normalized.governing_thought: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should fund the software business to profitability and keep quick commerce as a gated option
executive_summary: Answer: no. Quick commerce is a growing market without a profit pool. Launching would lose money on every order at every level of performance anyone has observed, breach the board's 12-month runway rule within the first year, and turn the grocers who buy our software into competitors. The software business can reach cash break-even inside current cash.
Market GMV grows ~42% a year ($1.8B → $5.1B, 2022–25), but both scaled incumbents lose $1.90–$3.40 per order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities
At benchmark-median inputs an order loses $2.67 before site costs and $6.17 after
The plan's +$2.02 per order needs all four levers above the best site ever observed; our own pop-up lost ~$12.60 per order
Pop-up customers do not repay their $38 acquisition cost at benchmark economics
The plan needs $9.5M of our $12.0M cash to month 18; no new round is expected
It breaks the ≥12-month runway rule by month ~1 (if on top of today's $0.4M/month burn) or ~11 (most favourable reading)
At benchmark economics nine mature sites would lose ~$18M a year, 1.5× our total cash
3 Software is the better use of the cash
Indicative model: cash break-even in ~26 months at today's 60% growth, cash never below $5.4M
Still works at 40% growth (break-even ~month 36); below ~30% costs must be cut
9 late-stage deals = $0.86M ARR; pipeline grocers want their own fast delivery from stores, so we sell them the tools rather than compete
Decisions requested: (1) decline the Parcelbird Now launch and its $5.4M capex; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; (3) adopt the quarterly re-entry triggers on page 13.

slides.title: We began with the founders' hypothesis and tested the five things that would have to be true for it to hold; only market growth survives

claims.claim: Market: Demand is growing fast — Holds
evidence: US quick-commerce GMV grew 41.5% a year, 2022–25 ($1.8B → $5.1B); every year was +38% or more

claims.claim: Unit economics: Orders make money at performance we can achieve — Fails
evidence: −$2.67 per order before site costs at benchmark median; positive only if AOV, promotions, rider productivity and density all beat the best site observed

claims.claim: Customers: Customers stay and order enough to repay their acquisition cost — Fails
evidence: 22% still ordering in month 3, at 3.1 orders a month; $173 of acquisition cost per retained customer is never repaid at benchmark economics

claims.claim: Capital: It can be funded from current cash with ≥12 months runway at all times — Fails
evidence: $9.5M of $12.0M needed to month 18; runway rule broken by month ~1–11; no new round expected

claims.claim: Right to win: Our software know-how gives an operating edge, and operating does not hurt the core business — Fails
evidence: Our pop-up ran below the benchmark median on every lever; pipeline grocers who want their own fast delivery would become competitors

claims.claim: Revised answer: do not launch. Growth alone does not make the case — the incumbents prove a growing market can still lose money on every order. Focusing on software is the only option that meets the board's constraints.

slides.title: Quick-commerce demand is growing ~42% a year, but the scaled incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating

evidence: US quick-commerce grocery GMV: 2022 $1.8B, 2023 $2.6B, 2024 $3.6B, 2025 $5.1B

claims.claim: The regional model is worse and shrinking: QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025.
evidence: QuickBasket (regional): Revenue $210M, EBITDA −$96M, margin −46%, contribution per order −$3.40

claims.claim: "Nobody owns the Midwest" is more plausibly a sign of poor economics in mid-size cities than of an open prize.

slides.title: Appendix 2: the runway, pop-up and software-path figures rest on simple calculations from the pack's numbers

claims.claim: Runway under the plan
evidence: Reading A: burn = $0.40M + $9.5M ÷ 18 = $0.928M a month. 12-month floor = $11.1M, reached after (12.0 − 11.1) ÷ 0.928 ≈ 0.9 months. Cash = 0 after 12.0 ÷ 0.928 ≈ 12.9 months.
Reading B: burn = $0.528M a month. Floor = $6.3M, reached after (12.0 − 6.3) ÷ 0.528 ≈ 10.7 months. Month 18 cash = $2.5M = 6.2 months at the $0.4M software burn.

claims.claim: Pop-up ramp
evidence: Loss ≈ 11,800 × −$12.57 ≈ −$148k (annualised fixed cost applied per order)

claims.claim: Software path
evidence: Today's total costs ≈ $4.1M revenue + $4.8M annual burn = $8.9M, of which cost of goods 19% × $4.1M = $0.78M and operating costs $8.12M; plus $0.8M hires = $8.92M
Break-even ARR = 8.92 ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M
60% → break-even month 26, low point $5.4M, minimum runway ≈24 months; 40% → month 36, $2.7M, ≈18 months; 30% → rule breached ≈ month 23

normalized.recommendation: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch and its $5.4M capex (do not launch in 2027; commit no dark-store capex); approve ≈$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; adopt a cash guardrail (≥12 months runway reviewed monthly, with a cost plan ready if trailing growth falls below 40%) and the quarterly re-entry triggers — revisit quick commerce only if all hold: a customer site sustains positive site-level profit for two quarters; rider minimum-pay rules in the target cities are settled and costed; the software business is cash-flow positive, or committed funding keeps ≥12 months runway after the launch budget.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch Parcelbird Now as planned (9 dark stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not recommended: path to profit only if all four levers beat the best site observed; runway rule breached by month ~1 to ~11; $9.5M budget and up to $18M a year of losses at median; competes with grocer customers.

alternatives_considered.option: B. One permanent pilot site (Columbus, 12 months, plus software plan)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not recommended: pilot loses ≈$2.0M a year at median and delays software break-even; lowest runway ≈10 months at 60% growth (breached); ≈$2.6M at risk; signals intent to compete; repeats the pop-up. "A single permanent site answers the wrong question: density is the uncertainty least able to rescue the economics."

alternatives_considered.option: C. Focus on software (incl. store-based fast-delivery tools for grocers)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: cash break-even ≈ month 26 (60% growth), ≈ month 36 (40%); lowest runway ≈24 months at 60%, ≈18 at 40%; ≈$0.8M a year for four hires; serves grocers' wish to launch fast delivery from existing stores.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Risk: Software growth slows — break-even ≈ m26 at 60%, ≈ m36 at 40%; rule breached ≈ m23 at 30%. Mitigation: monthly tracking; pre-agreed cost plan below 40% growth
Risk: A rival captures the Midwest while we wait. Mitigation: be in the market as supplier to grocers' own fast delivery; triggers allow re-entry
Risk: Our unit-economic inputs are wrong — benchmarks are 14 sites; mid-size Midwest density is unproven. Mitigation: re-run the model each quarter on customer-site data
Risk: Rider minimum-pay rules — +$1 an hour = $0.42 per order at median productivity. Mitigation: sell batching and dispatch efficiency as product value to grocers
Risk: Founder focus and morale — not quantifiable. Mitigation: channel ambition into the fast-delivery product line
Benchmark medians from 14 customer sites represent what a new Parcelbird site would achieve; the delivery fee is already net of payment cost.
The plan's $9.5M is spread evenly over 18 months (phasing not provided); runway is measured as cash ÷ current monthly burn.
Software costs stay at today's implied level (≈$8.1M a year excluding cost of goods) plus $0.8M of hires; ARR converts to revenue at 81% gross margin. Indicative model.
Rider-pay uplifts are illustrative: the pack gives no figure for the proposed minimum pay standards.
Customer payback ignores orders by churned customers in months 1–2 and any churn after month 3; the two partly offset.
Unclear whether the $9.5M includes the software business's $0.4M monthly burn; both readings shown.
Best observed column pairs best AOV and best density from different sites; treated as an upper bound.
Pop-up week-1 and week-6 volumes derived assuming steady 18% weekly growth summing to 11,800 orders.
Option B assumes one permanent site at benchmark-median economics for 12 months ($1.15M fixed cost, $0.6M capex).
Prepared without access to the briefing team; these choices are open for the board to challenge.
next_steps: Scope store-based fast-delivery tools (picking, batching, rider dispatch) with pipeline grocers that want to launch.
Turn the pop-up's lessons (promotions, rider productivity) into product features for customers.
Build a quarterly benchmark from the 14+ customer sites to track the triggers.
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text, so there were no images to view. Chart values on slides 4, 5, 7, 10 and 12 were rebuilt from loose labels in the text, and I paired labels with values by the order they appear in. On slide 3 the verdicts came as a separate list (Holds, Fails, Fails, Fails, Fails), and I matched them to the table rows in order. On slide 12 the 30% growth line shows only a $0.1M label, and its position on the chart is unclear. The numbers that open the slide 2 summary sections (1, 2, 3) were matched to the section headers by order.
